topic: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
parentTitle: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
title: 24-hour postural care
blurb: Protect body shape in lying, sitting and standing, explain the link to chest infections and swallowing, and keep postural plans going in every setting.
question: Lewis, 30, has a profound learning disability and very limited movement. Every night he lies on his right side with both knees dropped to the left, and his family have noticed his pelvis looks twisted. Why does this matter, and what should the nurse do?

teach.body: Postural care is an approach that aims to preserve and restore body shape and muscle tone for people with movement difficulties. People with profound and multiple learning disabilities often sit and lie in a few limited positions; over time, gravity and lack of movement cause predictable changes in body shape until they cannot move out of their preferred position. This is not inevitable: the right equipment and positioning can protect body shape. In plain English: how someone lies at night shapes their body by day.
teach.cite: PHE, Postural care and people with learning disabilities (2018)

teach.caption: A personalised 24-hour programme covers every position the person spends time in, day and night.

head: System
Problem
teach.caption: PHE: pneumonia is the most common cause of death in people with PMLD.

teach.body: The Confidential Inquiry into premature deaths of people with learning disabilities (CIPOLD) established a link between failure to protect body shape and premature death, and recommended commissioners provide proactive postural care. The LeDeR pneumonia review found 45% of people who died from pneumonia had postural problems, compared with 32% of those who died from other causes. Good postural management reduces respiratory risk factors such as poor airway clearance, saliva problems, reflux and thoracic deformity.
teach.cite: PHE postural care 2018; LeDeR pneumonia report 2024

teach.body: Person-centred outcomes matter (less pain, better sleep, dignity), but body symmetry measurements are fundamental. The Goldsmith Indices of Body Symmetry measure chest rotation, chest depth to width ratio, windsweeping and hip abduction, taken lying down so a poorly positioned chair does not distort them. In many people body shape tends to worsen over time, so keeping measurements stable is a good outcome.

Lewis spends hours each night in one asymmetric position: both knees falling to one side rotates his pelvis, a windswept pattern that leads to hip dislocation and spinal curvature. The nurse refers him to physiotherapy for a postural care assessment and night-time positioning. Lewis lacks capacity for this decision, so a best interests decision under the MCA is made with his family, considering comfort, sleep and the least restrictive option. His family are trained and supported, because PHE notes families can find night positioning hard at first.

teach.text: Postural care does not stop at the hospital door. PHE describes equipment being refused on admission for 'infection control' wrongly: equipment that belongs to one person should not raise those issues. Positioning needs belong in the hospital passport, and for longer stays the physiotherapist can write temporary guidelines, such as recreating support with pillows.

items: Recognise people at risk: limited movement, preferred postures, PMLD.
Refer early to physiotherapy or a postural care service.
Follow the plan for sitting, lying and standing across the 24 hours.
Train and support family carers and staff; explain why it matters.
Make sure positioning needs are in the hospital passport and followed on admission.
When dysphagia, constipation or chest infections recur, consider posture too.
Postural care preserves and restores body shape for people with movement difficulties.
24-hour programmes cover lying (including night), sitting, standing, handling and training.
Distortion causes hip dislocation, scoliosis, chest infections, dysphagia, constipation and pain.
CIPOLD linked failure to protect body shape with premature death; 45% of LeDeR pneumonia deaths had postural problems.
Measure symmetry lying down; keep plans going in hospital.

summary: You can now explain what 24-hour postural care is and why body shape distortion threatens breathing, swallowing and life expectancy. You can support positioning plans across settings, involve families and recognise when posture lies behind recurring health problems.

A.q: Carla, a learning disability nurse, is explaining 24-hour postural care to the family of Toby, 15, who has cerebral palsy and a profound learning disability. What is its main aim?
options: To increase muscle strength through daily exercise
To protect body shape in lying, sitting and standing
To reduce the need for regular pressure area checks each day
To help Toby walk independently by adulthood
A.why: Postural care aims to preserve and restore body shape and muscle tone across all positions, day and night.

whyNot.0: Exercise may help, but the aim is protecting body shape in every position.
whyNot.2: Postural care helps skin but does not replace pressure area care.
whyNot.3: Independent walking is not the aim; protecting body shape is.

A.q: Lewis, 30, has a profound learning disability. He sleeps every night on his side with both knees dropped to the same side. Which problem is he most at risk of developing?
options: Foot drop from nerve compression
Shoulder dislocation on the lower side
Pressure ulcers on both heels
Windswept hips with hip dislocation
A.why: Long periods with both knees falling to one side rotate the pelvis (windsweeping), leading to hip dislocation and spinal curvature.

whyNot.0: Foot drop is not the predictable change from this posture.
whyNot.1: Shoulder dislocation is not the typical consequence.
whyNot.2: Heel pressure is not the main risk of side-lying with knees dropped.

A.q: A support worker asks why postural care matters for preventing chest infections in Marie, 47, who has a profound learning disability and scoliosis. Which explanation is best?
options: Distorted body shape restricts the chest and airway clearance
Postural care keeps her warm and so prevents chest infections
Body shape changes weaken the immune response in the lungs
Repositioning removes bacteria that settle on the skin
A.why: Thoracic deformity, poor airway clearance, saliva problems and reflux are respiratory risk factors that good postural management can reduce (PHE 2018).

whyNot.2: The effect is mechanical, not immune.
whyNot.3: Skin bacteria are not the link to chest infection.

B.q: Ben, 22, has a profound learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about night-time positioning. His physiotherapist recommends a positioning system. His mother is unsure. What should happen?
options: The physiotherapist decides and fits it the same week
A best interests decision involving his mother and physio
Ben's mother signs consent on his behalf as next of kin
The system is put on hold until Ben can decide for himself
B.why: Night positioning can restrict movement, so for a person lacking capacity it needs a best interests decision under MCA 2005 s4, consulting family and considering the least restrictive option.

whyNot.0: Professionals consult family and record a best interests decision; they do not decide alone.
whyNot.2: A parent cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.
whyNot.3: Delay allows body shape to worsen; best interests decisions exist for this situation.

B.q: Ruby, 38, has a profound learning disability and has been in her wheelchair for six hours at a day centre. Her postural care plan says to change position every two hours. What should staff do?
options: Leave her as she looks comfortable and settled
Tilt her chair back for the rest of the afternoon
Reposition her out of her chair as the plan sets out
Ask her family to reposition her when they collect her
B.why: Prolonged sitting in one position increases pressure damage and body shape distortion; the plan's schedule should be followed.

whyNot.0: Appearing settled does not mean her body shape and skin are protected.
whyNot.1: Tilting is not a change out of her chair and is not the plan.
whyNot.3: The plan applies in every setting, not only at home.

B.q: A nurse reviewing the postural care of Hassan, 19, who has cerebral palsy, wants to know whether his body shape is being protected. Which measure is most useful?
options: Monthly weight on a sit-on scale
Body symmetry measured while lying
Daily pain scores on a numerical scale
His seated height in his wheelchair
B.why: Body symmetry measurements such as the Goldsmith Indices, taken lying down, show whether body shape is stable or changing.

whyNot.0: Weight does not show body shape change.
whyNot.2: Pain matters, but it does not measure symmetry.
whyNot.3: Seated measures are distorted by chair positioning.

C.q: Grace, 26, has a profound learning disability and scoliosis and is admitted with a chest infection. Her mother brings her night positioning system, but a staff nurse says it cannot be used because of infection control. What should the registered nurse do?
options: Agree and use pillows in a standard side-lying position
Send the equipment home and request a hospital system
Use her own system and follow her home postural plan
Ask her mother to stay overnight to position her by hand
C.why: Continuing the established postural plan is a reasonable adjustment that protects body shape and breathing. PHE notes equipment belonging to one person should not raise infection control issues.

whyNot.0: Standard positioning may not protect her body shape or chest.
whyNot.1: Sending it home leaves her without support while a substitute is found.
whyNot.3: Her mother may help, but the ward remains responsible for following the plan.

C.q: Sam, 35, has a profound learning disability. He has had recurrent chest infections and constipation, and staff are treating each episode separately. He spends most of the day in one reclined position. What is the best next step?
options: Ask for a 24-hour postural care assessment
Request a stronger regular laxative from the GP
Arrange long-term antibiotics to prevent infections
Increase his fluids and repeat the chest X-ray
C.why: PHE: dysphagia and constipation can be caused or worsened by body shape distortion, but the link is often missed. With movement difficulties, posture should be considered and referred.

whyNot.1: Laxatives treat a symptom without addressing posture.
whyNot.2: Antibiotics treat infection but not the underlying cause.
whyNot.3: This repeats acute treatment and misses the underlying issue.

C.q: A family find night-time positioning difficult: their son, 17, wakes more and they worry he is uncomfortable. They want to stop using it. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell them it must be used every night without fail
Agree to stop, as the family know him best
Explore their concerns and arrange physio support
Report the family for failing to follow the plan
C.why: PHE notes families often need considerable support when starting night positioning (sleep, repositioning, comfort, temperature). Listening and arranging practical support helps them continue safely.

whyNot.0: Insisting without support ignores real problems and loses trust.
whyNot.1: Stopping without exploring options risks progressive body shape change.
whyNot.3: Difficulty with equipment is not neglect; it calls for support.

reteach.title: Gravity never sleeps
reteach.question: Why do a few hours each night in one position matter so much over years?

blocks.body: A person who cannot move themselves lies in the same position for hours every night, sits the same way every day. Gravity slowly pulls the knees, pelvis and spine into that shape. Over years the chest twists, hips dislocate and swallowing and breathing get harder. Supporting symmetrical positions across the 24 hours slows or prevents this.

blocks.text: Recurrent chest infections, dysphagia or constipation in someone with movement difficulties: ask about posture, not only about antibiotics and laxatives.

explain.body: A personalised 24-hour programme: adaptive seating, positioning equipment for lying including at night, moving and handling techniques, and training for family carers and professionals.

test.q: Which positions does 24-hour postural care cover?
options: Sitting and standing in the daytime
Lying at night and sitting at meals
Lying, sitting and standing
Standing during physiotherapy sessions
test.why: Postural care addresses all body positions the person adopts across the day and night: lying, sitting and standing.

whyNot.0: Night-time lying is a key part.
whyNot.1: Standing and wider daytime sitting are also covered.
whyNot.3: It is a 24-hour approach, not one session.

explain.body: Hip dislocation, contractures, spinal curvature, swallowing problems, constipation, reflux, pressure sores, pain, fatigue and depression. Respiratory problems are the main reason people with PMLD need medical care.

test.q: According to PHE, what is the most common cause of death in people with profound and multiple learning disabilities?
options: Pneumonia
Cancer
Heart disease
Epilepsy
test.why: PHE (2018): respiratory problems are the main reason people with PMLD need care, and pneumonia is the most common cause of death in this group.

whyNot.1: Cancer is a leading cause overall, but PHE names pneumonia for PMLD.
whyNot.2: Heart disease is common but not the most common in PMLD.
whyNot.3: Epilepsy contributes to risk but is not named as the commonest cause.

explain.body: CIPOLD linked failure to protect body shape with premature death. LeDeR (2024): 45% of people who died from pneumonia had postural problems vs 32% of those who died of other causes.

test.q: Which inquiry established a link between failure to protect body shape and premature death in people with learning disabilities?
options: Death by Indifference
Winterbourne View review
Francis Inquiry
CIPOLD
test.why: PHE (2018) cites CIPOLD as establishing the link and recommending proactive postural care services.

whyNot.0: Death by Indifference described six deaths but is not the source of this finding.
whyNot.1: Winterbourne View concerned abuse in an inpatient unit.
whyNot.2: The Francis Inquiry concerned Mid Staffordshire.

explain.body: Positioning needs go in the hospital passport. Own equipment should come with the person. Physiotherapists can write temporary guidelines for longer stays.

test.q: Where should a person's positioning needs be recorded so hospital staff can follow them?
options: In the GP's referral letter
In the hospital passport
On the drug chart
In the discharge summary
test.why: PHE: hospital passports should include how the person needs to be positioned at different times, such as eating, drinking and at night.

whyNot.0: Referral letters may not reach ward staff or cover daily care.
whyNot.3: The discharge summary is written at the end of the stay.
